Welcome to our newsletter!

Hi, I'm Max Roser, the founder and co-director of Our World in Data.

As part of our newsletter community, you're set to receive data-driven insights and explanations of the key trends shaping our world, right to your inbox.

This is a great way to learn more about the world and how it's changing, keep up to date with our latest work, and find entry points into our rich catalog of data and research. I hope you enjoy it!

What to expect in your inbox

You'll receive an email when we publish new work matching your preferences:

Topics: {{topics}}

Content types: {{contentTypes}}

Frequency: {{frequency}}

You can update your preferences or unsubscribe from topic notifications at any time.

Who we are

Our World in Data (OWID) is a free, open-access website that makes data and research on the biggest global challenges easier to access and understand, to empower those working to build a better world.

OWID is a collaborative effort between researchers at the University of Oxford and the UK-based charity Global Change Data Lab. Learn more about our mission, funding, team, and more.

Global data and research on 120+ topics

We bring together high-quality data on more than 120 topics, such as poverty, CO₂ emissions and climate change, migration, democracy, global health, population growth, armed conflicts, and artificial intelligence.

Our researchers and data scientists help you understand these topics, writing explanations that describe the data, what it shows, and why it matters.

We make it easy to explore this data in over 14,000 interactive charts and maps and 30+ data explorers — all free to reuse under our permissive Creative Commons license. You can also embed interactive versions of our charts on any website.

We've also made it easy to download and reuse the data in our charts.

Read more about our mission and key ideas

Why do we need to know about progress if we are concerned about the world's largest problems?

The world is awful. The world is much better. The world can be much better.

The limits of our personal experience and the value of statistics

The short history of global living conditions and why it matters that we know it

Thanks for subscribing!

I truly hope you enjoy our newsletter. If you do, please consider sharing it with others who you think would find it useful — they can subscribe here. If you have any questions or feedback, just reply to this email.

Wishing you all the best,
Max
